bib.title: Clean Code, Chapter 7: Error Handling
bib.venue: Robert C. Martin, Clean Code: A Handbook of Agile Software Craftsmanship, Prentice Hall (printed pp. 103-112; the PDF carries a www.it-ebooks.info footer)

question: How should code handle errors so that it is both clean and robust, with error handling kept separate from the main logic?
hypothesis: Error handling that obscures logic is wrong; treating it as a separate concern makes code readable and robust at once.

results.claim: Error handling that obscures the logic of the code is wrong.
results.setup: Java examples; general principle stated in the chapter opening.
results.quote: Error handling is important, but if it obscures logic, it’s wrong.

results.claim: Throw exceptions instead of returning error codes or flags, because codes clutter the caller and are easy to forget to check.
results.setup: Listing 7-1 (nested if/else on handle and status) versus Listing 7-2 (sendShutDown with try/catch around tryToShutDown), Java DeviceController.
results.quote: it is better to throw an exception when you encounter an error. The calling code is cleaner.

results.claim: A try block defines a transaction-like scope: the catch must leave the program consistent however the try aborts, so write the try-catch-finally first and drive it with a test that forces the exception.
results.setup: TDD example: retrieveSection test expects StorageException on an invalid file name; catch is first Exception, then narrowed to FileNotFoundException.
results.quote: In a way, try blocks are like transactions.

results.claim: Checked exceptions are not worth their price in general application development: a low-level throws clause cascades signature changes upward and breaks encapsulation. The chapter names Python among the languages with no checked exceptions.
results.setup: Java argument; the Open/Closed Principle citation is [Martin] 2002. Feathers concedes checked exceptions can help in a critical library.
results.quote: Neither do Python or Ruby. Yet it is possible to write robust software in all of these languages.

results.claim: Each exception should carry context (the failed operation and the type of failure) because a stack trace cannot say what the operation intended.
results.quote: a stack trace can’t tell you the intent of the operation that failed.

results.claim: Define exception classes by how they are caught; wrap a third-party API so it raises one common exception type, which removes duplicated catch blocks, limits dependency on the vendor and eases mocking. Use separate classes only when a caller wants to catch one and let the other through.
results.setup: ACMEPort wrapped by LocalPort, which translates three exception types to PortDeviceFailure.
results.quote: wrapping third-party APIs is a best practice.

results.claim: Special Case Pattern: return an object that encodes the exceptional case (per diem meal expenses, an empty list) so the client has no special branch.
results.source: Fowler (Special Case Pattern; no reference entry printed)
results.setup: ExpenseReportDAO returns PerDiemMealExpenses instead of throwing MealExpensesNotFound; getEmployees returns Collections.emptyList().
results.quote: That behavior is encapsulated in the special case object.

results.claim: Do not return null: it creates null-check clutter for callers and one missed check breaks the application. Throw or return a special case object, and wrap null-returning third-party methods.
results.setup: registerItem example with nested null checks, Java.
results.quote: the problem is that it has too many.

results.claim: Do not pass null: neither an InvalidArgumentException nor an assert gives the handler a good action, so forbid null arguments by default.
results.quote: the rational approach is to forbid passing null by default.

results.claim: Error handling should be treated as a separate concern that can be reasoned about independently of the main logic.
results.quote: Clean code is readable, but it must also be robust.

limits: Java-only examples; no data or measurements, every result is an assertion by the author.
Written in 2008 for Java; the checked-exception debate and null guidance do not transfer one-to-one to Python (no checked exceptions; None is idiomatic for 'absent').
The chapter does not cover context managers, try-with-resources, logging levels, retries or error handling in async code.
The Special Case Pattern is credited to Fowler with no reference entry; the Bibliography lists only [Martin] 2002.
practices: Throw exceptions rather than return error codes or flags (p. 104).
Write the try-catch-finally first and use a test that forces the exception to build the transaction-like scope (p. 105-106).
Do not use checked exceptions in general application code (p. 106-107).
Put the failed operation and failure type in the exception message, and pass enough to log in the catch (p. 107).
Define exception classes by how callers catch them; often one class per area is enough (p. 107-109).
Wrap third-party APIs to map their exceptions to one local type (p. 108-109).
Use the Special Case Pattern so normal flow needs no exception handling (p. 109-110).
Do not return null; return an empty collection or a special case object (p. 110-111).
Do not pass null as an argument (p. 111-112).

terms.definition: You create a class or configure an object so that it handles a special case for you. When you do, the client code doesn’t have to deal with exceptional behavior.

lineage.work: Martin, Agile Software Development: Principles, Patterns, and Practices, Prentice Hall, 2002
lineage.note: Cited for the Open/Closed Principle in the checked-exceptions argument.
Named as [Fowler] on p. 110; not in the printed bibliography.

problems: Byline is Michael Feathers, not Robert C. Martin.
Text uses ligature glyphs (fi) and curly quotes; quotes in this file avoid ligature words.
Listing 7-2 is split across pages 104-105 and the layout interleaves with the 'Write Your Try-Catch-Finally Statement First' text in the extraction order.
Some printed code has typos (missing semicolon, 'peristentStore', 'throw InvalidArgumentException(' without new); not corrected here.
